chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Post-2008 and Post-COVID Regimes

lessons.title: The 2013 Taper Tantrum: Imported Inflation and the Rupee Under Pressure

children.text: On 22 May 2013, in a Congressional testimony in Washington DC, Fed Chair Ben Bernanke said the Fed could eventually start slowing, or tapering, its bond-buying programme if the US economy kept improving. He did not announce any actual policy change that day. Within about ten weeks, the Indian rupee had lost roughly a fifth of its value against the dollar. A sentence about a future possibility, from a central bank on the other side of the world, was enough to trigger one of the sharpest currency shocks in modern Indian history.

body.text: The 2013 taper tantrum was not primarily an Indian policy failure. It was a global liquidity shock that landed hardest on the economies foreign investors judged most vulnerable, and India, running a record current account deficit at the time, sat close to the top of that list.

body.title: Ten Weeks That Shook the Rupee

events.title: Bernanke's "Taper Talk"
events.description: The Fed Chair signals the possibility of eventually slowing QE bond purchases. Global investors, who had parked large sums in emerging market bonds and currencies chasing yield during years of ultra-loose Fed policy, begin pulling money out in anticipation.

events.title: The Rupee Hits an All-Time Low
events.description: The rupee falls from around ₹55 per dollar in May to a record low near ₹68.8 per dollar by late August, a fall of roughly 20-25% in about three months. Morgan Stanley analysts label India, Brazil, Indonesia, South Africa and Turkey the "Fragile Five", economies most exposed to a reversal of foreign capital flows.

events.title: Raghuram Rajan Becomes RBI Governor
events.description: Rajan, a former IMF chief economist, takes over mid-crisis and moves quickly, launching a special FCNR(B) deposit swap window days later to attract fresh foreign currency inflows from non-resident Indians.

events.title: The Rupee Stabilizes
events.description: Combined with gold import curbs and improving investor sentiment, the measures work: the rupee stabilizes, and India's current account deficit narrows sharply from its crisis-era peak within about a year.

stats.label: Rupee, Late Aug 2013
stats.context: An all-time low at the time

stats.label: India's CAD, FY2012-13
stats.context: A record high, the core vulnerability

children.text: A current account deficit means a country is spending more on imports, and other outflows, than it earns from exports and other inflows, and has to fund that gap somehow. India's gap, driven heavily by gold and oil imports, had widened to a record roughly 4.8% of GDP going into 2013, and a meaningful part of it was being funded by foreign portfolio flows into Indian debt and equity markets, the kind of capital that can leave in weeks rather than years. When the taper talk raised the prospect of higher US yields pulling global capital back toward the US, investors reassessed exactly which emerging markets were most dependent on that footloose money to fund their deficits. India's large CAD made it an obvious answer.

The response combined a new governor's credibility with a specific, targeted toolkit rather than blunt, economy-wide rate hikes. The centrepiece was a special swap window allowing banks to raise foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians (FCNR-B deposits) and swap them with the RBI at an attractive rate, which is widely cited as having pulled in upward of $25 billion in fresh dollar inflows within months, directly rebuilding the reserves and confidence the rupee needed. Alongside this, the government raised import duties on gold multiple times and introduced rules requiring a portion of imported gold to be re-exported, directly targeting the CAD's biggest single driver. The RBI had also briefly tightened short-term liquidity just before Rajan's arrival, a defensive move to make rupee speculation more expensive.

cells: Attracted fresh NRI dollar deposits by offering banks an appealing RBI swap rate, rebuilding reserves
Raised the cost of India's single biggest non-essential import, directly targeting the CAD
Required a share of imported gold to be re-exported rather than consumed domestically
Made it costlier to bet against the rupee by raising short-term borrowing costs

body.text: Notice how much of the rupee's stabilization happened before the FCNR(B) inflows had even fully arrived. Rajan's appointment itself, given his international standing, is widely credited with calming markets on sentiment alone. This is the same credibility mechanism from the Volcker and RBI-framework lessons earlier in this course, just compressed into weeks instead of years: a credible messenger can move markets before a single policy measure has actually taken effect.

children.text: This is the third time in this course you have seen this exact mechanism: 1966, 1991, and now 2013, a sharp rupee depreciation directly raising the cost of everything India imports, oil most of all, since India imports well over three-quarters of its crude requirement. That is a textbook cost-push shock, and it landed on top of the double-digit CPI inflation environment from the last lesson, making an already difficult inflation picture worse. The rupee's fall meant Indian consumers effectively paid a double inflation tax through this period: elevated domestic price pressure from before, plus a fresh, currency-driven layer on top of it.

body.title: Do the Pass-Through Math
body.prompt: Global crude oil is trading at $100 a barrel. The rupee weakens from ₹55 to ₹68 per dollar, while the dollar price of oil does not move at all. What is India's new rupee cost per barrel?
body.explanation: ₹68 x $100 = ₹6,800 per barrel, up from ₹5,500 before the depreciation, a rise of about 24%, purely from the currency move, with no change in the dollar oil price at all. This is exactly why a sharp rupee depreciation acts as a direct, immediate cost-push shock on an oil-importing economy like India.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why was India included in Morgan Stanley's "Fragile Five" grouping during the 2013 taper tantrum?
options: India had defaulted on its foreign debt
India's rupee was fixed to the US dollar at the time
India ran a large current account deficit funded significantly by footloose foreign portfolio flows, making it vulnerable to a reversal in global capital
India had just introduced capital controls banning all foreign investment
body.explanation: The "Fragile Five" label was about external vulnerability: large current account deficits funded by capital that could leave quickly. It had nothing to do with a default or a fixed exchange rate, India's rupee floats, and everything to do with how exposed the funding of that deficit was to a shift in global investor sentiment.

points: The 2013 taper tantrum began with words, not action: a single Fed testimony about a future possibility was enough to trigger a sharp emerging-market selloff.
India's record current account deficit, funded significantly by footloose portfolio capital, made it one of the "Fragile Five" economies most exposed to that shock.
Rajan's FCNR(B) swap window, gold import curbs, and his own credibility as a new governor combined to stabilize the rupee within months.

A sharp currency depreciation is a direct cost-push, imported-inflation mechanism, the same pattern seen in India's 1966 and 1991 devaluations, now layered onto an already elevated domestic inflation environment.
This episode fed directly into the institutional reforms from the last chapter; the next lesson picks up a very different kind of global inflation shock, the 2021-22 post-COVID surge.
